los.text: Describe the main causes, pathophysiology, diagnosis, sites and type of pneumonias (bacterial, viral and atypical)
los.html:
PneumoniaInfection of lung parenchyma → alveoli fill with exudate (consolidation).
Classification by settingCommunity-acquired (CAP), hospital-acquired (HAP, ≥48 h after admission), ventilator-associated, aspiration, immunocompromised.
TypeOrganismsClues
Typical bacterialStreptococcus pneumoniae (commonest), H. influenzae (COPD), S. aureus (post-influenza, cavitating), MoraxellaAcute onset, high fever, productive (rusty) sputum, pleuritic pain, lobar consolidation
AtypicalMycoplasma (young, cold agglutinin haemolysis, erythema multiforme), Legionella (air conditioning, ↓Na⁺, deranged LFTs, diarrhoea), Chlamydophila pneumoniae/psittaci (birds), Coxiella (Q fever, farm animals)Gradual, dry cough, extrapulmonary features, patchy/interstitial CXR; don't respond to β-lactams (no cell wall/intracellular)
ViralInfluenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSVSeasonal, myalgia; bacterial superinfection
HAPGram-negatives (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli), MRSARecent hospitalisation, ventilation
AspirationAnaerobes, oral floraStroke, alcohol, ↓GCS; right lower lobe
ImmunocompromisedPneumocystis jirovecii (HIV CD4 <200), fungi, CMV, TB
  • Pathophysiology (lobar): congestion → red hepatisation (RBCs, neutrophils, fibrin) → grey hepatisation → resolution.
    • Bronchopneumonia: patchy, centred on bronchioles, often bilateral bases (elderly, debilitated).

los.text: Describe the clinical presentation and the main investigations undertaken to determine the cause of common respiratory infections (including imaging, culture, Mantoux test, QF Gold; focus on pneumonia)
los.html:
Clinical
  • Cough, sputum, fever, breathlessness, pleuritic pain
  • Confusion in elderly.
  • Signs: tachypnoea, tachycardia, dull percussion, bronchial breathing, crackles, ↑ vocal resonance over consolidation.
Severity
  • CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >7, RR ≥30, BP SBP <90 or DBP ≤60, age ≥65): 0–1 home, 2 consider admission, ≥3 severe (consider ICU).
  • In primary care CRB-65.
  • NEWS2.
Investigations
  • CXR: consolidation (air bronchograms), effusion, cavitation; repeat at 6 weeks if smoker/>50 to exclude underlying cancer.
  • Bloods: FBC, U&E, CRP, LFT; blood cultures; ABG if hypoxic.
  • Sputum MC&S; urinary antigens (pneumococcal, Legionella) in moderate/severe; viral PCR; Mycoplasma PCR/serology.
  • TB: sputum acid-fast bacilli smear (Ziehl–Neelsen/auramine) ×3 + culture (gold standard, 2–6 weeks; liquid culture) + NAAT (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance; CXR (upper lobe cavitation); bronchoscopy/BAL if no sputum.
  • Latent TB tests: Mantoux (tuberculin skin test) (intradermal PPD; induration at 48–72 h; false positive after BCG/NTM) and IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) (blood test of T-cell IFN-γ release to TB-specific antigens; not affected by BCG). Neither distinguishes latent from active disease.
  • CT chest for complications (empyema, abscess).

los.text: Describe the management of pneumonia, including drug treatment
los.html:
CAP antibiotics (NICE NG138/BTS)
  • Low severity (CURB-65 0–1): amoxicillin 500 mg TDS × 5 days (doxycycline or clarithromycin if penicillin-allergic).
  • Moderate (2): amoxicillin + clarithromycin (atypical cover).
  • High (3–5): IV co-amoxiclav + clarithromycin (or levofloxacin if allergic).
  • Review at 48–72 h; switch IV to oral; total ~5 days if improving.
HAPEarly, non-severe → co-amoxiclav; late/severe → broader (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam) per local guidance ± MRSA cover (vancomycin/linezolid).
AspirationCo-amoxiclav (anaerobic cover).
LegionellaMacrolide or fluoroquinolone. PCP: high-dose co-trimoxazole + steroids if hypoxic.
SupportiveO₂ (target 94–98%; 88–92% if CO₂ retainer), fluids, analgesia (pleuritic pain), VTE prophylaxis, physiotherapy, nutrition; escalate (NIV/ventilation) if failing.
ComplicationsParapneumonic effusion/empyema (drain), lung abscess, sepsis, ARDS, AF.
AdviceSymptoms resolve over weeks (cough ~3 weeks, fatigue up to 6 months); smoking cessation; vaccines (pneumococcal, flu).

los.text: Describe the clinical presentation and management (include drug treatment) of TB
los.html:
Pathogen
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast, slow growing, airborne droplet nuclei). ~¼ of the world has latent infection
  • UK cases concentrated in people born in high-incidence countries, homeless people, prisoners, drug/alcohol users, immunosuppressed (HIV, anti-TNF).
Primary TB
  • Ghon focus (lower/mid zone) + hilar lymph nodes = Ghon complex
  • Usually contained (granulomas with caseous necrosis) → latent TB.
  • Children/immunosuppressed → progressive or miliary TB, TB meningitis.
Post-primary/reactivationUpper lobes (high O₂), cavitation. Symptoms: chronic cough >3 weeks, haemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy.
ExtrapulmonaryLymph node (scrofula), pleural, spinal (Pott's disease), genitourinary (sterile pyuria), meningitis, pericarditis, abdominal.
Drug treatment of active TB (RIPE)
  • 2 months rifampicin + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + ethambutol, then 4 months rifampicin + isoniazid (6 months total; 12 months for CNS TB, plus steroids).
  • Directly observed therapy if adherence concerns.
DrugKey side effects
RifampicinOrange body fluids, hepatitis, CYP450 inducer (↓ OCP, warfarin, steroids, antiretrovirals)
IsoniazidPeripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine), hepatitis
PyrazinamideHepatotoxicity, gout (↑ urate)
EthambutolOptic neuritis (red–green colour vision: check acuity before)
  • Baseline LFTs, U&E, visual acuity
    • HIV test all TB patients.
    • Notifiable disease.
    • Isolate (airborne precautions) until 2 weeks of treatment if smear-positive.
    • MDR-TB (resistant to rifampicin + isoniazid): longer regimens (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid: BPaL/M).
  • Latent TB treatment (to prevent reactivation): 3 months rifampicin + isoniazid or 6 months isoniazid.

los.text: Explain how current therapies and contact tracing have evolved in line with TB spread throughout the years
los.html:
Pre-antibiotic era
  • TB ("consumption", "White Plague") was a leading cause of death in 19th-century Europe
  • Sanatorium movement (rest, fresh air, nutrition)
  • Surgical collapse therapy (artificial pneumothorax, thoracoplasty).
  • Mortality began falling before drugs, due to improved living conditions, nutrition, less overcrowding (McKeown).
Key milestones
  • Koch identifies M. tuberculosis (1882)
  • BCG vaccine (1921; UK schools programme 1953–2005, now targeted to high-risk infants)
  • Streptomycin (1944)
  • → rapid resistance with monotherapy
  • → combination therapy (first MRC RCT in 1948 showed streptomycin; PAS + streptomycin reduced resistance)
  • → isoniazid (1952)
  • → rifampicin (1960s)
  • → short-course 6-month regimen (1970s–80s)
  • → DOTS strategy (WHO 1990s).
ResurgenceHIV co-infection (1980s–90s), migration, homelessness, drug resistance (MDR/XDR-TB). WHO declared a global emergency (1993); End TB Strategy (2015).
  • Contact tracing evolved from household screening to systematic concentric circle approach: test close (household) contacts first, extend if transmission found
  • Screening with symptoms, CXR, IGRA/Mantoux
  • Treat latent TB
  • New-entrant screening for migrants from high-incidence countries
  • Whole-genome sequencing now tracks transmission chains and resistance.
Modern toolsRapid molecular diagnostics (GeneXpert), shorter regimens for drug-sensitive (4-month) and resistant TB (6-month BPaL), video-observed therapy.

los.text: Describe the key components and developmental processes of the respiratory system
los.html:
Week 4
  • Respiratory (laryngotracheal) diverticulum buds from the ventral foregut (endoderm → epithelium and glands; splanchnic mesoderm → cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, vessels).
  • Tracheo-oesophageal septum separates trachea from oesophagus (failure → TOF/oesophageal atresia).
Lung bud divides into bronchial buds: right gives 3 lobes, left 2.
Stages of lung development
StageWeeksEvents
Embryonic4–7Lung buds, lobar and segmental bronchi
Pseudoglandular5–17Branching to terminal bronchioles; no gas exchange possible (congenital diaphragmatic hernia here → hypoplasia)
Canalicular16–26Respiratory bronchioles, vascularisation; type II pneumocytes appear, surfactant starts ~24 weeks → viability limit
Saccular26–36Terminal sacs, thin walls, more surfactant
Alveolar36 weeks – ~8 yearsMature alveoli; most alveoli form after birth
Surfactant deficiency(preterm)Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome: antenatal corticosteroids accelerate maturation; exogenous surfactant.
Fetal breathing movements and amniotic fluid are needed for lung growth (oligohydramnios → pulmonary hypoplasia, e.g. renal agenesis/Potter sequence).
At birthFluid cleared (adrenaline-driven Na⁺ absorption, compression in labour) → first breaths → ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance.

los.text: Describe bacterial pathogenicity and the main signs and symptoms observed in patients
los.html:
• Pathogenicity = ability to cause disease; virulence = degree.
  • Steps and virulence factors:
    • Adherence: pili/fimbriae (UPEC P-fimbriae → pyelonephritis), adhesins.
    • Invasion: invasins, enzymes (hyaluronidase, collagenase, streptokinase in S. pyogenes).
    • Evading immunity (capsule): anti-phagocytic: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae b, Klebsiella (hence asplenia risk).
    • Evading immunity (other): protein A (S. aureus), IgA protease, antigenic variation, intracellular survival (Mycobacterium, Listeria, Salmonella), biofilms.
    • Iron acquisition: siderophores.
    • Damage (exotoxins): secreted, specific proteins: cholera, tetanus, botulinum, diphtheria, TSST-1 (superantigen), C. difficile toxins A/B, Shiga toxin.
    • Damage (endotoxin): LPS/lipid A of gram-negatives → TLR4 → TNF, IL-1 → fever, septic shock, DIC.
  • Signs and symptoms reflect local damage (pus, abscess: S. aureus; spreading cellulitis: S. pyogenes) and systemic response (fever, rigors, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion = sepsis).
    • Toxin-mediated disease can occur without invasion (food poisoning by preformed S. aureus/B. cereus toxin: rapid vomiting).
  • Koch's postulates (with molecular modifications) link organism to disease.
